result.summary: A run of fragments from the Catalogue of Women covers heroines and heroes of Thessaly, Boeotia and Aetolia. It touches Iphiclus the runner, the gifts of Dionysus, Coronis and the death of Asclepius, Cyrene, Antiope, Dodona, and Meleager's family with Deianeira.

scenes.title: Clymene's son Iphiclus and others
scenes.summary: Clymene marries Phylacus and bears the swift Iphiclus, who can run over ears of corn without bending them. Short notes on Thoas and Maro follow.

scenes.title: Gifts of Dionysus
scenes.summary: Wine is a joy and a sorrow; the heavy drinker is bound by it and sleeps.
scenes.stakes: Drunkards lose control of hands, feet, tongue and wits.

scenes.title: Coronis and Asclepius
scenes.summary: Coronis lived by Lake Boebias; a crow tells Phoebus she has wed Ischys. Zeus kills Asclepius with a thunderbolt, and Apollo is punished, though Leto intercedes.
scenes.stakes: Apollo risks being cast into Tartarus by Zeus.

scenes.title: Cyrene and Aristaeus
scenes.summary: Cyrene is praised for her beauty, and her son Aristaeus is named.

scenes.title: Antiope and the walls of Thebes
scenes.summary: Antiope grows up in Hyria; Zethus and Amphion build Thebes' walls with a lyre.

scenes.title: Dodona and its oracle
scenes.summary: Ellopia is described, and Zeus's oracle at Dodona in an oak, where men bring gifts to ask prophecy.

scenes.title: Meleager and Deianeira
scenes.summary: Meleager is praised for slaying the Calydonian boar and dies fighting the Curetes. Althaea's children are listed, including Deianeira, who unknowingly does a fearful thing with the poisoned robe.
scenes.stakes: Meleager dies in battle; Deianeira's ignorance brings doom to Heracles.

scenes.title: Lamentation for Oedipus
scenes.summary: Argeia and others come to mourn Oedipus after he dies in Thebes.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a title of Apollo; the text uses both names.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid description of wine's binding power over the drunkard.
Famous image of Iphiclus running over wheat without bending it.

analysis.text: The fragments catalogue heroines and their offspring, linking mortal families to gods and heroic stories, as the Catalogue of Women does throughout.
These lines survive only as quotations in scholars and papyri, showing how ancient writers used Hesiodic genealogy as a source for myth.

legacy.text: The tale of Coronis, the crow and Asclepius's death was retold by Pindar and later Ovid.
Deianeira's poisoned robe became the subject of Sophocles' Women of Trachis.

fun_facts.text: Fragment 98 comes from a Berlin papyrus, one of the ancient scrolls that preserve parts of the otherwise lost Catalogue.

language_notes.text: The claim is hyperbole of speed: Iphiclus is said to outrun the winds and skim across grain without bending it.
Asphodel is a pale lily-like plant; here its 'fruit' means its seed-heads, which Iphiclus would not crush.
'Binds together' with 'fetters unspeakable' describes drunkenness as being tied up; 'unspeakable' means beyond description.
'Unshorn' is Apollo's standing epithet: he is the eternally youthful god who never cuts his long hair.
Pytho is the older name of Delphi, site of Apollo's oracle.
'Son of Leto' here means Apollo, though the sentence's subject is Asclepius' death; the quote is probably garbled, since Zeus killed Asclepius and angered Apollo.
Apollo's servitude to a mortal refers to his service to Admetus, king of Pherae, as punishment for killing the Cyclopes who made Zeus's thunderbolt.
Aristaeus was a rustic god of beekeeping, herding and farming; Virgil invokes him in the Georgics.
Hyria was a Boeotian town; Antiope, mother of Zethus and Amphion by Zeus, is placed there as a young girl.
"Glebe" means soil or cultivated land; "kine" is an old plural for cattle; "shambling" describes their slow, rolling walk.
The doves refer to the sacred doves of Dodona, whose rustling and cooing in the oak were traditionally interpreted as the god's answers.
The "(?)" marks a doubtful reading in the damaged papyrus; the translator is guessing the missing words.
Apollo is said to have slain Meleager, though other versions say he died through his mother Althaea's curse and the burning brand.
The poisoned robe refers to the garment steeped in the centaur Nessus's blood, which Deianeira sent to Heracles and which killed him.

context_notes.text: Scholiasts were ancient commentators whose marginal notes preserve fragments of lost poems like the Catalogue of Women.
In the usual story the crow was white until it brought Apollo this news; the angry god then turned it black.
Asclepius, Apollo's son, was a healer who grew so skilled that Zeus struck him down for raising the dead.
Tartarus is the deepest pit of the underworld, where Zeus imprisoned his enemies.
The Graces were goddesses of charm and beauty, so likeness to them is high praise.
Amphion's lyre was said to be so enchanting that stones moved into place by themselves to form the walls of Thebes.
Dodona in Epirus was one of the oldest Greek oracles, where Zeus's will was sought through the sacred oak.
The Calydonian boar was sent by Artemis to ravage Calydon; Meleager's killing of it was a famous heroic hunt.
Argeia, daughter of Adrastus, was the wife of Polynices, Oedipus's son, so her mourning ties the families of Thebes and Argos.

literary_notes.text: Racing the winds and treading grain without bending it exaggerates Iphiclus' speed to mythic extremes.
'A joy and a sorrow both' sums up wine's double nature in one balanced phrase.
Wine acts as a violent person who seizes and binds the drinker, then lulls him with 'soft sleep' that embraces him.
The water is shaped like a mountain, as when a river forms a wall of water to shelter a visitor.
The question stresses Meleager's fearsomeness by implying that no mortal but Heracles would dare face him.
Fire shining from his eyes gives a vivid, supernatural picture of Meleager's fierce, almost divine, warrior nature.
"Black doom" and the fearful act done in ignorance hint at the coming tragedy of Heracles's death, with dramatic irony in Deianeira's innocence.
